Regulatory Transformation

Regulatory Transformation: navigating emerging risks, driving AI adoption and reducing regulatory burden

Regulators are facing a shifting operating environment as technology, markets, environmental pressures and societal expectations evolve faster than traditional regulatory frameworks. Fragmented data and limited intelligence continue to make risk prioritisation difficult.

There is a growing opportunity to use advanced analytics to better target regulatory effort. Many regulators are still working to integrate data across systems, uplift analytical capability and embed insights into everyday decision-making.

AI adoption is also becoming a core regulatory transformation issue. Regulators are seeking to balance opportunities for automation and improved risk identification with the need to manage governance, transparency, bias, legal risk, privacy and public confidence.

At the same time, governments are under pressure to reduce red tape, make faster decisions and manage fiscal constraints. This is driving interest in regulatory consolidation, shared-service models and more consistent approaches to regulatory delivery, while maintaining fairness and strong outcomes.

Regulation Hub Intelligence Brief

AI Brief 123 articles across 8 categories

The fortnight is shaped by three converging regulator investment themes: APRA and ASIC are jointly recalibrating the Financial Accountability Regime through active consultation, compressing the window for accountability-mapping and governance-gap engagements across ADIs and insurers; the AG's Department Privacy Reform Taskforce and the sanctions framework overhaul are simultaneously in open consultation, signalling that Commonwealth agencies and regulated entities need implementation architecture support before both cycles move to legislation; and enforcement intensity is escalating across consumer markets (ACCC digiDirect $99k penalty), financial services (APRA v BAB personal liability ruling, ASIC licence cancellations), and border controls (ABF depot shutdowns in illicit tobacco), confirming regulators are in active penalty mode rather than guidance mode. Clients in the news include John Holland (Comcare Metro charges), ANU (TEQSA registration conditions), and digiDirect (ACCC misleading pricing), each carrying live regulatory exposure with assurance and advisory hooks. The merger regime's parliamentary fine-tuning and the CSLR omnibus passage add implementation complexity across advice licensees and M&A-active clients that the sector has not yet absorbed. KPMG's immediate BD priority is the FAR consultation window — a time-bounded, multi-entity accountability-mapping engagement with a clear regulatory anchor and demonstrable PEPI credentials. The secondary priority is privacy and sanctions reform, where the Commonwealth is actively building implementation architecture and PEPI has established entry points across AG's Department, Home Affairs, and the defence export base.

Cross-category themes

Across all categories, regulators are simultaneously escalating enforcement (ASIC, APRA, TEQSA, Ahpra, ESC, ABF, NHVR) while opening consultations that signal imminent structural reform, creating a dual advisory pressure where clients face immediate compliance remediation alongside forward-looking framework redesign. The clearest cross-cutting pattern is expanded personal and organisational liability, with director accountability (FAR, APRA/BAB), practitioner standards uplift (Ahpra), provider registration tightening (NDIS, TEQSA), and export controls all converging on governance adequacy as the primary compliance test.

AI Brief16 articles

The fortnight is defined by three converging enforcement-to-legislation cycles that signal significant advisory demand: illicit tobacco enforcement is scaling to new legislative powers (ABF depot shutdowns, Labor modelling excise cuts, Police and Customs gaining new enforcement tools), creating implementation and change-management pull-through across Border Force and state police; the ACIC has lodged a submission to the PJCIS signalling an active intelligence-capability review with likely gaps in data-sharing, technology, and workforce that KPMG can position against; and the eSafety Commissioner's first empirical report on the social-media minimum-age regime confirms the regulation is entering an implementation stress-test phase, with the August 2026 symposium indicating eSafety is actively seeking external expertise on monitoring and enforcement architecture. AUSTRAC's professional designated-services expansion and the AFP's joint-agency corrupt-conduct charge (APS employee) reinforce a broader integrity and AML/CTF compliance uplift cycle across Commonwealth agencies.

In parallel, engage the eSafety account lead to position a compliance-architecture or assurance offer ahead of the next reporting cycle, given the Commissioner is publishing early-days findings that explicitly flag implementation gaps.

Tech & AI

The Australian government is actively courting big tech to co-design internet safety and AI regulatory frameworks, signalling that legislative architecture is being drafted now — KPMG's window to shape design-phase governance work is open and closing fast. Simultaneously, AI enforcement credibility is under direct attack: the WhichCar and NT News reporting on 6,500 incorrect AI-issued traffic fines exposes a systemic gap in human-oversight and explainability controls within state government AI deployments, a wound that will drive urgent remediation procurement. CASA's Part 138 digital integration via myCASA and Airservices Australia's 2026-27 Corporate Plan both signal aviation regulators embedding digital transformation into core operational cycles, expanding the addressable market for KPMG's technology risk and assurance offering in safety-critical environments. EPA Victoria's sensor deployment initiative in Latrobe Valley points to environmental regulators scaling IoT and real-time data infrastructure, a precursor to AI-driven compliance monitoring that will require privacy, data governance and assurance capability. The dominant client signals this fortnight are federal government (AI regulation design), state transport authorities (AI error remediation), CASA, Airservices Australia, and EPA Victoria. KPMG PEPI's strongest hooks are responsible AI frameworks, AI assurance and explainability, and digital transformation advisory for safety-critical regulators.

Capability reviews

Learning & development

Three Commonwealth and cross-jurisdictional clients are simultaneously activating workforce capability agendas this fortnight, signalling a coordinated uplift cycle rather than isolated programs. Comcare is expanding return-to-work (RTW) initiatives, reflecting pressure on Commonwealth agencies to reduce workers' compensation liabilities and demonstrate rehabilitation outcomes — an area where KPMG's workforce health and regulatory compliance capability is directly applicable. DEWR's Free TAFE expansion is accelerating, with the department now administering significant VET funding flows that require implementation governance, data reporting frameworks, and outcome measurement — all live advisory gaps. Risk & assurance

Six regulators are simultaneously in active enforcement or framework-uplift mode this fortnight, a density that signals a structural lift in public-sector compliance investment rather than a routine cycle. APRA's litigation against BAB directors is the highest-consequence signal: personal liability is now a tested remedy, and every APRA-regulated board needs a governance gap assessment before the next enforcement action names their members. Ahpra is the most active single regulator across three concurrent tracks — peptide prescribing enforcement, a practitioner codes-of-conduct consultation, and the IPCP accreditation framework rollout — making health a priority sector for integrated assurance mandates. The Aged Care Quality and Safety Commission's active recovery of Higher Everyday Living Fees from providers signals that the ACQSC is moving from monitoring to enforcement, and aged care clients carrying fee-setting risk need a compliance health-check now. AUSTRAC's professional designated services expansion extends AML/CTF obligations deeper into accounting and legal — our own sector — which creates both a compliance uplift mandate for professional services clients and a credibility conversation on what robust AML assurance looks like. The NDIS reform agenda and Australia's sanctions framework overhaul each represent multi-year assurance and compliance architecture opportunities where KPMG's regulatory and risk capability has direct relevance. Across all six, the common thread is regulators converting policy frameworks into enforcement actions, which compresses client preparation time.

Australian Health Practitioner Regulation AgencyAustralian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines AuthorityAged Care Quality and Safety Commission

State-gov priorities

Cited strategic priorities across all 9 jurisdictions, refreshed bi-annually. Every source URL is .gov.au.

Housing supply is the dominant cross-jurisdictional policy commitment, with every state and territory carrying a major homes target — from VIC's 800,000 by 2034 and QLD's 1 million by 2046 through to TAS's 10,000 affordable homes by 2032 — creating parallel demand for planning reform advisory, social housing financial modelling, and delivery program assurance across all eight clients simultaneously. A second near-universal theme is domestic industrial policy: CTH's Future Made in Australia ($22.7B), WA's Made in WA fund, NSW's onshoring of manufacturing, SA's State Prosperity Project, and NT's resource-sector growth strategy all signal a coordinated, if uncoordinated, shift toward supply-chain resilience and critical minerals, where KPMG can offer investment facilitation, industry capability assessments, and trade and competitiveness advisory. Defence is a concentrated opportunity: CTH's $330B Integrated Investment Program, WA's Defence West 2025-2040 strategy, and NT's defence-sector priority are mutually reinforcing and create sustained demand for procurement advisory, workforce planning, and industry participation frameworks over a 15-year horizon. Energy transition and hydrogen diverge sharply by jurisdiction — SA targets 100% net renewable electricity by 2027 and has a funded hydrogen facility, TAS aims for 200% renewable generation by 2040, and ACT is building toward net zero by 2045, while NT explicitly prioritises fossil-fuel-adjacent resource sectors, meaning KPMG must hold differentiated advisory positions across the client base rather than a single net-zero narrative. Justice and community safety reform is a distinct cluster in NT (Crime Reduction Strategy 2024-2027), QLD (Making Queensland Safer Act 2024, youth justice), and NSW (DFV Safer Pathway rollout), each with legislated timeframes and implementation risk that suits program assurance and evaluation engagements. CTH's aged care transition to Support at Home (live from November 2025, CHSP migration by July 2027) and VIC's decade-long mental health Royal Commission implementation are the two largest human services reform programs nationally, both requiring capability uplift, change management, and benefits realisation support at scale. The strongest BD angle cutting across all jurisdictions is long-horizon infrastructure strategy: ACT, SA, WA, and TAS all have 20-year strategies in active update cycles, NSW and QLD are executing major transit programs, and none have resolved the gap between strategy documents and delivery governance — a repeatable offer in business case development, benefits management frameworks, and independent assurance.

Last refreshed 2026-07-01. Bi-annual schedule; source URLs verified to .gov.au.
